This work deals with the challenging problem of evaluating the abstract visual reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). There has been a recent interest in the Bongard problems and how these can still stump the so-called advanced visual models, mostly due to a lack of reasoning. This work is another step towards the direction of showing that there exist inherent limitations in MLLMs that make them fail in abstract reasoning tasks.

Overall, the paper generated a good discussion among the authors and the reviewers, and most reviewers leaned towards (weakly) accepting the paper at the end. The AC wants the authors to closely look at the remarks of Reviewer Gh92 while preparing the camera-ready version of the paper, especially the following points:

1. The work demonstrates relatively poor human baseline performance, which might point to unwanted ambiguity in the dataset. Potential ambiguity coupled with reduced dataset scale might make it hard to draw useful conclusions when ranking different models or in trying to understand model failures to guide future improvement.

2. The real efficacy of the multi-class classification setup since not many details were provided in the rebuttal regarding the same, as well as no human baseline results were provided for this setup.

I recommend weak acceptance for this work.
We would like to thank the Reviewer for the comments. We are glad to see the positive rating of our paper.

We would like to thank the Reviewer for the comments.

> Novelty: The only novelty are the Bongard-RWR problems. These problems are interesting, but, the scope is …

Thank you for recognizing the novelty of the introduced benchmark. While the construction of RWR itself is a key contribution of our work, we would like to emphasize that the novelty extends beyond that, and has been acknowledged by several Reviewers.

RWR is designed to complement the existing landscape of BP datasets. This enables the comparison between synthetic BPs and RWR, which highlights the increased difficulty of recognizing abstract concepts in real-world images, where visual factors such as colour, texture, or perspective introduce additional ambiguity. Furthermore, contrasting model performance on RWR with that on other BP-related datasets such as HOI and OpenWorld reveals that while MLLMs perform well when concepts are directly grounded in real-world scenarios, they struggle with recognizing more abstract concepts. BPs from RWR do not merely test recognition of common real-world objects or actions, but require identifying nuanced concepts in a contextual way, aligning more closely with evaluations of fluid intelligence. 

Moreover, the 10 solution strategies formulated in our work offer a systematic approach to characterizing model abilities and are in our opinion a general contribution to the AVR field in the context on MLLM utilization. As shown in Fig. 4 (top), the GT and IL binary classification strategies help analyze model biases in accepting or rejecting candidate answers. Table 1 illustrates model preferences across three distinct manually designed solution strategies, each reflecting a different problem-solving approach. Fig. 5 demonstrates how effectively models utilize information from the visual modality (left) and dialog context (right). Additionally, during the rebuttal, we introduced 3 new RWR variants, featuring square images, greyscale images, and their combination, which help to further diagnose model robustness. Altogether, we believe the evaluation framework presented in our work provides a comprehensive approach for assessing models’ abstract reasoning capabilities. 

Our work includes a diverse evaluation across both open-access and proprietary MLLMs, and a human study establishing a baseline under the free-form setting, recognized as a valuable contribution by several Reviewers.

We hope that the paper can be positively assessed in light of all the above contributions which extended beyond the sole Bongard-RWR dataset preparation.

> Dataset size: I agree that the quality of the dataset is very high, but having only 100 samples will severely limit any conclusions that we can draw from the performance on the dataset.

While the current dataset size is limited, we note that the original BPs were also expanded iteratively over time in small increments (Foundalis, 2006b). This is caused by an extreme difficulty in providing new BP concepts, which requires manual effort and creativity. Our benchmark represents the first step toward real-world representations of synthetic BPs, and we welcome contributions from the community to grow and improve the Bongard-RWR dataset in a way similar  to the development of the original Synthetic Bongard dataset.

We would like to thank the Reviewer for the comments.

> The authors mentioned …

We would like to clarify that in multiclass classification, the set of candidate answers for each BP was constructed dynamically. For each problem instance, the incorrect answer choices were taken from subsequent matrices that referred to different concepts. In effect, there was no fixed set of 16 concepts repeated in this experiment, which helped in preventing bias toward any particular subset of concepts.

Human performance was evaluated under a different setup. Participants provided a free-form textual description of the relevant concept, which was then assessed by expert annotators.

While a direct comparison is challenging due to different evaluation setups, the 65% average human accuracy in the free-form setup is roughly comparable to the performance of SOTA models, InternVL2.5 78B and Qwen2-VL 72B, in the multiple-choice setup with only 4 candidate answers (see Tables below). This suggests that current models struggle to match human-level performance, revealing a substantial gap in their reasoning capabilities. It also highlights the relative difficulty of RWR compared to HOI and OpenWorld, which primarily require recognition of concrete objects or interactions.

**InternVL2.5 78B**

|:----------|-----:|-----:|-----:|
| hoi       | 1.00 | 0.99 | 0.99 |
| openworld | 0.99 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| rwr       | 0.88 | 0.65 | 0.38 |
| synthetic | 0.86 | 0.83 | 0.70 |

**Qwen2-VL 72B-Instruct**

|#concepts  |   2  |   4  |  16  |
|:----------|-----:|-----:|-----:|
| hoi       | 1.00 | 0.99 | 0.96 |
| openworld | 0.98 | 0.98 | 0.97 |
| rwr       | 0.85 | 0.67 | 0.32 |
| synthetic | 0.91 | 0.69 | 0.41 |

> While I agree …

We fully agree that open-ended BP solutions are subject to subjective interpretation. Anticipating this, our scoring methodology explicitly accommodated such ambiguity. All human responses were evaluated by 2 experts and categorized into four classes:
1. incorrect concept
2. different concept than expected, but an acceptable interpretation
3. concept closely related to the expected one
4. expected concept

Unanimous scores of 1 or 4 were accepted directly, and all other cases were discussed among annotators until a consensus was reached, so as to handle the inherent subjectivity and ambiguity in open-ended descriptions.

Given the open-ended nature of the task, we believe that 65% mean accuracy of humans is reasonable. Each RWR instance was solved by at least one participant, with the best-performing individual solving 59 out of 60. Half of the respondents solved more than 40 problems (two-third), and no participant solved fewer than 23 (Fig. 7). The problems exhibit varying levels of difficulty (Fig. 8) and participants rated it as rather difficult (Fig. 6). Bongard-RWR poses a challenge even for humans, but we argue that this level of difficulty is desirable due to the rapid progress in MLLM reasoning capabilities.

> More generally, … 

We agree that disentangling perception and abstraction is inherently difficult – as Hofstadter (1995) argued, these capabilities are deeply intertwined in human cognition. In the paper, we adopt this perspective and don’t explicitly attempt to decouple these 2 aspects. Nevertheless, we believe that the overall contribution of our paper can meaningfully guide future research.

First, the comparison between synthetic BPs and RWR highlights the increased difficulty of recognizing abstract concepts in real-world images, where colour, texture, or perspective introduce additional ambiguity. Second, comparing model performance on RWR with that on HOI and OpenWorld reveals that MLLMs struggle with recognizing more nuanced concepts in a contextual way, which aligns more closely with fluid intelligence.

Moreover, the 10 solution strategies formulated in our work offer a systematic and general framework for assessing MLLM reasoning capabilities. In Fig. 4 (top), the GT and IL binary classification strategies help analyze model biases in accepting / rejecting candidate answers. Table 1 illustrates model preferences across three distinct manually designed solution strategies, each reflecting a different problem-solving approach. Fig. 5 shows how effectively models utilize information from the visual modality (left) and dialog context (right). Additionally, during the rebuttal, we introduced 3 new RWR variants, featuring square images, greyscale images, and their combination, which help to further diagnose model robustness.

While the current dataset size is limited, we note that the original BPs were also expanded iteratively over time in small increments (Foundalis, 2006b). This is caused by an extreme difficulty in providing new BP concepts, which requires manual effort and creativity. Our benchmark represents the first step toward real-world representations of synthetic BPs, and we welcome contributions from the community to grow and improve the dataset.

Dear Reviewer, we are grateful for your insightful comments and suggestions, which helped us to improve the paper. 

> The first claimed contribution is confusing: …

Thank you for this comment. We will rephrase this statement. Prior work on BP benchmarks has primarily focused on pre-trained image encoders with few-shot classifiers, rather than comprehensively evaluating MLLMs. While Wu et al. (2024) did assess GPT-4V on Bongard-OpenWorld, they did not compare it to other MLLMs. Furthermore, prior work has primarily framed BPs as a binary classification task. Wu et al. (2024) consider an explicit concept generation setup in their appendix, but use standard NLP metrics for evaluation, making it difficult to assess model accuracy in solving BPs. In contrast, we systematically evaluate a set of proprietary and open-access MLLMs in both binary classification and open-ended generation settings across 4 datasets comprising both synthetic and real-world images.

> … negative pairings …

For the negative pairings in the binary classification setup, we assigned each BP instance a negative concept from a different BP. Specifically, for a given BP instance $i$, we selected the concept from BP $(i + 20) mod 100$. We manually reviewed the resulting pairings to confirm that the selected negative concept was distinct from the original concept. Thank you for bringing this point to our attention. We shall include the above description in the revised version of the paper.

> For the open-language setup, …

Given the scale of our experiments (the number of datasets, problem instances, models, and generation strategies), manual assessment of every response is infeasible. Hence, in Section 3.2 we proposed an automatic assessment strategy. To improve its robustness, we carefully selected the best-performing evaluation models based on a manual review of selected evaluations and tuned the evaluation prompt to align results with human assessments (Appendix E). While open-ended answer evaluation remains an open problem in NLP research, Tables 3 and 4 in Appendix E show high consistency between our final evaluation pipeline and scores of human experts.

Furthermore, in the evaluation process we did not rely on a single model judgement, but instead evaluated the answers in the mixture-of-experts manner, with the voting scheme of 4 MLLMs manually optimized in preliminary experiments.

> … formulated as multiple-choice …

Please, see our response to Reviewer Aobr (the last paragraph of *“… concurrent work, …”*).

> … examples where the models and humans disagree …

Responses from human participants were evaluated by expert annotators, who compared them to ground-truth labels and classified them as correct or incorrect. This final binary assessment was used to compute the average human accuracy. No manual corrections were made to their answers.

In Appendix E.2 (Tables 3  and 4) we compare the evaluations of the proposed MLLM ensemble with human experts. The voting approach achieves high consistency with human experts, scoring 99% and 90% for synthetic BPs and Bongard-OpenWorld, resp. Figures 11 and 12 highlight cases where the evaluations differed. High agreement rates suggest that an automated evaluation is sufficiently robust and well-suited for the scale of experiments conducted in our study.

> The human baseline …

Please, see our response to Reviewer NTSJ (*“Another concerning factor is that human performance …”*).

> … human participants were given all examples …

Participants were given all 60 examples in a document and asked to submit their responses via a form. They had full control over the order in which they solved the problems and could allocate as much time as needed for each question. Figure 6 (top-right) shows the amount of time spent by participants, as reported in the closing survey. On average, respondents spent between 1 and 2 hours to complete the challenge. Since the participants were free to choose the order of problem-solving, we do not have sufficient data to systematically analyze the influence of fatigue or boredom on performance. However, this flexibility likely helped mitigate such effects, as participants could distribute their effort based on individual preferences.

> Other works relevant …

Thank you for pointing out these relevant works. KiVA focuses on visual analogical reasoning inspired by developmental psychology, evaluating how models generalize visual transformations. Perception Test assesses multimodal video understanding across various reasoning tasks. In contrast, our work investigates abstract visual reasoning through Bongard Problems, spanning both synthetic and real-world domains. Our setting differs from both KiVA and Perception Test by focusing on contextual visual analogies rather than perceptual transformations or video understanding. These works assess MLLM reasoning capabilities from different angles and we view them as complementary. We will reference both papers in Section 2.

Dear Reviewer, we are grateful for your insightful comments and suggestions, which helped us to improve the paper. 

> … the novelty … is not clear.

In preliminary experiments, we observed that while MLLMs perform well on HOI and OpenWorld, they struggle with Synthetic BPs. We identified two key factors distinguishing Synthetic from HOI and OpenWorld. Firstly, Synthetic feature simple 2D geometric shapes, while HOI and OpenWorld consist of real-world images. A potential explanation might be that the lack of training data on synthetic images could contribute to the lower performance on Synthetic BPs. Secondly, Synthetic focus on abstract concepts (e.g., “One line vs. Two lines”), while HOI and OpenWorld involve concepts grounded in the real world (e.g., “A person jumping on a surfboard vs. Not a person jumping on a surfboard”). This led us to hypothesize that MLLMs may find abstract concepts harder to recognize.

This motivated us to create Bongard-RWR, which bridges the gap between these two domains by representing abstract concepts with real-world images. Apparently, RWR presents a major challenge to contemporary MLLMs, despite relying on real-world images. This indicates that abstract concepts are inherently difficult for models to recognize regardless of their representation. We hope this summary clarifies the novelty of Bongard-RWR over the existing benchmarks.

> … relation to prior work …

We discuss the motivation for Bongard-RWR in Section 1 and in Section 2 position our work within AVR tasks and approaches to solve BPs. We further elaborate on recent trends and future directions in Appendix A. If the Reviewer finds any aspect of this discussion missing, we would greatly appreciate specific pointers to improve the paper accordingly.

> … the limited size of the benchmark.

Please, see our response to Reviewer 2kYM (*“The sample sizes are relatively small …”*).

> Are there any structural differences …

Figure 22 summarizes per model Bongard-RWR results. Notably, 38 problems remain unsolved by any model, while 8 problems were solved by at least 3 models: #2, #7, #10, #23, #32, #57, #88, and #100. These BPs encompass the following concepts: Large vs. Small figures, Figures elongated vertically vs. horizontally, Triangles vs. Quadrangles, One vs. Two figures, A sharp vs. No sharp projection, Identical vs. Not identical figures, Three vs. Five parts, and The letter A vs. B. Analysis of specific models reveals that Claude 3.5 Sonnet correctly solved 3 tasks concerning the distinction between triangles and other shapes (#10, #97, #98), suggesting that concepts involving object shapes are better recognized by the model. Other models do not present clear result patterns, and generally struggle with concept abstraction in BPs.

> In Figure 4, …

In the human study, participants were asked to express the rule in natural language. Their responses were then evaluated by expert annotators, who compared them to ground-truth labels and classified as correct / incorrect. This final binary assessment was used to compute accuracy. Since the human evaluation setup differs from the classification task in Figure 4, a direct comparison may be misleading. Instead, we will add human performance in the right-most section of Table 1, which concerns Bongard-RWR scores.

> … clarify the input resolution …

Single images were provided to the models at their original resolution. Whole problem matrices were constructed using the original images and then resized such that the longer edge (height or width) did not exceed 1024px, while keeping the aspect ratio fixed.

> … some SOTA models are missing …

Please see our response to Reviewer 2kYM (*“other strong open models”*).

> … analyze the effect of the prompt …

We manually optimized prompts based on preliminary results. The final prompts, shown in Appendix I, reflect these optimizations. For instance, this process led us to add to Prompt 6 “The description of the rule should be simple and concise.” along with two examples, adjusting the order of JSON fields in Prompt 7 (generate an explanation and concept before the binary answer), and adding guiding sentences in Prompt 10 (Descriptive strategy).

In addition, we manually reviewed selected model responses and found that models generally followed the task correctly, except for rare cases where they explicitly stated an inability to detect a concept or classified test images as belonging to neither side in the Images to Sides strategy. Such refusals indicate that models correctly interpreted the instructions but lacked the necessary visual reasoning capabilities.

> …  qualitative examples in the main paper, …

Due to space constraints, we could not fit qualitative examples in the main paper. However, Appendix H and Figures 23 – 26 provide qualitative examples that illustrate the challenges of Bongard-RWR, contrast it with synthetic BPs, and showcase specific problem instances alongside model responses.

Dear Reviewer, we are grateful for your insightful comments and suggestions, which helped us to improve the paper. 

> … feed multiple (sub-)images from group A or B all at once …

Thank you for this valuable suggestion. We explored this approach in preliminary experiments but the results were not promising. Feeding in all images separately significantly increases the input context length, often exceeding the limit supported by the employed MLLMs. Even when models could process longer image sequences, their performance remained weak in this setup. We suspect this is due to the scarcity of multi-image training of MLLMs. 

> The sample sizes are relatively small …

Bongard-RWR was designed with significant manual effort, as detailed in Section 4.1. Of 100 synthetic BPs considered, only 12 were automatically represented in the real-world domain using Algorithm 1 (Appendix F). The remaining problems required manual intervention, including translating abstract concepts to the real-world domain, selecting appropriate images, or photographing manually constructed scenes. This ensures that the dataset captures fine-grained abstract concepts, such as “Ends of the curve are parallel vs. Ends of the curve are perpendicular” or “Extensions of segments cross at one point vs. Extensions of segments do not cross at one point”, which are challenging to represent with real-world images. The fine-grained nature of the synthetic BPs made even a manual translation problematic in certain cases. For instance, in problems #77 (Angle divided in half) or #99 (Outlines made by triangles and circles intersect), we could not come up with a proper implementation of these specific concepts in the real-world domain. For such instances we abandoned their “imperfect’” representation, to preserve the indisputability of translated concepts in the Bongard-RWR dataset.

In contrast, Bongard HOI and Bongard-OpenWorld datasets, which were generated automatically using existing data sources, focus on coarse-grained concepts such as “A person jumping on a surfboard. vs. Not a person jumping on a surfboard”. While this automated process enables larger sample sizes, it limits the representation of fine-grained abstract concepts. 


> … other strong open models …

In Appendix D, we analyse the impact of scaling model size on the model’s performance, evaluating larger InternVL2 variants (up to 76B params) and LLaVa-NeXT (up to 110B params). Figure 9 shows that proprietary models still consistently outperform open-access ones. 

Prompted by this feedback, during the rebuttal phase, we evaluated 3 recent open-access MLLMs: InternVL-2.5 78B (AA), Qwen2-VL 72B (BB), and LLaVA-NeXT 110B (CC), on all 4 considered datasets using 3 binary classification strategies described in Section 3.3. The models were selected based on the integration readiness within our evaluation framework (LLaMa 3.2 vision is unavailable in our geographic location). 
* Ground-truth and Incorrect Label
  * AA improved significantly over InternVL2 8B, which was biased towards rejecting the tested concept (Figure 4, top row). The newer and larger variant achieves competitive performance to proprietary models (69/82, 83/99, 78/100, 17/55 with GT/IL for Synthetic, HOI, OpenWorld, and RWR, resp.).
  * BB slightly underperformed AA on the first 3 datasets but excelled on RWR, scoring 36/50, and was the leader in terms of the total score (86 vs. 81 for GPT-4o, the 2nd best model).
  * CC showed decent but lower performance compared to AA and BB.
* Images to Sides
  * BB performed best across the first 3 datasets, being on-par with proprietary models on HOI and OpenWorld, solving 96 problems in both cases.
  * On RWR, CC performed best, solving 24 problems, on par with Claude 3.5 Sonnet, the best-performing proprietary model on this dataset.

We shall add the above scaling results to Appendix D.

> What does Bongard Problems have to offer more than existing AVR benchmarks?

The motivation for using Bongard Problems is outlined in Section 1, where we highlight their unique challenge: solving BPs requires identifying an underlying concept expressed through images and articulate it in natural language. The requirement of expressing the answer in natural language forms a fundamental distinction from other AVR tasks. Moreover, the limited number of samples in BPs forces a few-shot learning setup, as opposed to typically large training datasets used for other AVR tasks (e.g., the most commonly considered Raven’s Progressive Matrices). Additionally, in the “AVR tasks” paragraph in Section 2, we discuss how BPs compare to existing AVR benchmarks, emphasizing that BP datasets considered in our work besides presenting a few-shot learning challenge, also cover both synthetic and real-world images, and enable both binary classification and open-ended answer generation. Appendix A extends this discussion, outlining future research directions for extending our research to other AVR tasks.

Dear Reviewer, we are grateful for your insightful comments and suggestions, which helped us to improve the paper. 

> … some easy adjustments to the dataset …

Thank you for these excellent suggestions regarding the dataset improvement. One of the key motivations behind Bongard-RWR is to test how models handle real-world complexity, which naturally includes variations in aspect ratio, resolution, and layout. Unlike synthetic BPs, real-world images are not uniformly structured and our dataset reflects this challenge. For instance, unifying image aspect ratios would require forceful rescaling, potentially introducing distortions or loss of content, which we aimed to avoid. Similarly, we refrained from cropping images, as doing so could obscure crucial visual features necessary for identifying abstract concepts. When arranging BP images into a joint matrix, we optimized the layout to minimize empty space between images.

In the Descriptive, Descriptive-iterative, Contrastive and Contrastive-iterative strategies, images are processed in their original resolution. In these cases, differences in resolution do not pose an issue, as the tested models are naturally capable of processing images of varying size. Also, differences in separators are not relevant, as the separator is not required in these settings. In the remaining strategies, we acknowledge that constructing joint BP images introduces some structural differences between Bongard-RWR and synthetic BPs. We believe, however, that variable aspect ratios, resolutions and picture layouts better align with the intention of reflecting the real-world variability in Bongard-RWR instances. 

At the same time, we fully agree that a rigorous, in terms of image formatting, comparison of synthetic and real-world instances could also lead to meaningful conclusions from a slightly different perspective. Toward this end, following the Reviewer’s suggestions, we constructed 3 new dataset variants featuring square images (RWR-S), greyscale images (RWR-G), and square greyscale images (RWR-SG). In square image variants, we manually cropped all images to square format and rescaled to 512x512 resolution. The full BP matrix was resized to 1024px width, maintaining aspect ratio, leading to 763px height.

We evaluated the 4 open-access models from the main paper and 3 additional large open-access models introduced during the rebuttal (InternVL-2.5 78B, Qwen-VL 72B, and LLaVA-NeXT 110B) in 3 binary classification setups from Section 3.3. In Ground-truth and Incorrect label settings, all models performed similarly on RWR and the 3 new variants. In Images to Sides, however, model performance differed:
* RWR-G: Most models solved slightly more problems compared to RWR, e.g. for Phi 3.5V (+15), Qwen2-VL 72B (+5), and LLaVA-NeXT 110B (+5). We hypothesize that since synthetic BPs are black-and-white, removing color in their real-world counterparts in RWR reduces unnecessary variation, making the task easier.
* RWR-S: The difference was even more pronounced, e.g. for InternVL2 8B (+13), InternVL2.5 78B (+9), Pixtral 12B (+9), LLaVA-NeXT 110B (+9), and Phi 3.5V (+7). We think that cropping increased the signal-to-noise ratio, by eliminating empty space and irrelevant background details.
* RWR-SG: Results aligned with the above trends, e.g. for InternVL2 8B (+11), InternVL2.5 78B (+8), Pixtral 12B (+7), LLaVA-NeXT 110B (+8), and Phi 3.5V (+17).

We will include the above results in the paper’s appendix and will release these new dataset variants alongside the main dataset. Once again, thank you for this excellent comment.

> The discrepancy between the dataset sizes …

Thank you for raising this point. We reported the results in raw counts to simplify their interpretation for Bongard-RWR, but we acknowledge that percentages may simplify comparisons across datasets. We will switch to percentages in the revised version. 

> … confuse the reader in Figure 4 …

We agree that differences in dataset sizes may affect the clarity of Figure 4. Using percentages would allow the random baseline to be consistently placed at 50%. We will revise the paper accordingly.

> … how the 100 problems of the larger datasets have been selected …

The selection of 100 problems from the larger datasets was driven by the need to balance diversity and computational feasibility. To ensure high instance diversity, we performed stratified sampling based on problem concept labels, selecting instances from the test splits on Bongard HOI and Bongard-OpenWorld. We will add the above clarification to the main paper in Section 5. Furthermore, as detailed in Section 3.2, our evaluation relies on an MLLM voting committee with 4 proprietary models, making inference costs scale with the number of datasets, problem instances, models, and generation strategies. Given these constraints, running multiple experiments on different random subsets was not feasible within our research budget.

We will include [1] in Section 2, as we agree it’s a relevant contribution.

While [1] explore a related topic, our work differs in several important ways. Their study evaluates vision language models (VLMs) on the first 100 synthetic BPs in two setups:

Open-ended language generation, which aligns with our Direct strategy. Likewise, they use an LLM-based judge to assess responses. Multi-class classification, where the VLM selects the correct concept from a predefined list.

We conduct experiments on 3 additional datasets, including Bongard HOI, Bongard-OpenWorld, and Bongard-RWR, the latter being a novel contribution of our work. Our main experiments cover 8 models, compared to 5 in [1]. We analyze the impact of model scaling on abstract reasoning capabilities (Appendix D), and examine model performance differences between synthetic and real-world BPs (Appendix H).

In summary, we believe that due to the above-discussed differences between [1] and our paper our work should be of value to the research community, despite the recent publication of [1].

rebuttal.value:
Dear Reviewer, we are grateful for your insightful comments and suggestions, which helped us to improve the paper. 

> The proposed test set is limited to 60 examples.

Please, see our response to Reviewer 2kYM (*“The sample sizes are relatively small …”*).

> Previous research has explored a similar task [1], …

Please, see our response to Reviewer Aobr (*“… concurrent work, …”*).

> The dataset generation and evaluation heavily rely on MLLMs, …

We appreciate the Reviewer’s concern regarding potential MLLM hallucinations and inaccuracies. We recognize this as an important challenge and have taken several steps to mitigate its impact on both dataset generation and evaluation.

For dataset generation, we implemented a rigorous manual verification process to ensure correctness of all problem instances, as detailed in Section 4 and Appendix F. Of the 100 synthetic BPs considered, only 12 generated instances were incorporated into Bongard-RWR without modification, while 24 required manual (human) adjustments, and 24 were constructed manually, entirely from scratch. Given this manual review of each Bongard-RWR matrix, we are confident that hallucinations and inaccuracies do not affect the final dataset quality.

Given the scale of our experiments (the number of datasets, problem instances, models, and generation strategies), manual assessment of every response is infeasible. For automatic evaluation, we acknowledge that relying on MLLMs introduces challenges. Hence, in Section 3.2 we proposed an automatic assessment strategy. To improve its robustness, we carefully selected the best-performing evaluation models based on a manual review of selected evaluations and tuned the evaluation prompt to align results with human assessments (Appendix E). While open-ended answer evaluation remains an open problem in NLP research, Tables 3 and 4 in Appendix E show high consistency between our final evaluation pipeline and scores of human experts.

Furthermore, in the evaluation process we did not rely on a single model judgement, but instead evaluated the answers in the mixture-of-experts manner, with the voting scheme of 4 MLLMs manually optimized in preliminary experiments.

> Another concerning factor is that human performance …

We would like to clarify that the reported 39.2 out of 60 refers to the average number of problems solved, which corresponds to 65% accuracy. Given the open-ended nature of the task, we believe this to be a reasonable score.

As detailed in Appendix B, every Bongard-RWR instance was solved by at least one human participant, with the best-performing individual solving all but one problem instance (59 out of 60). Furthermore, half of the respondents solved more than 40 problems (two-third), and no participant solved fewer than 23 instances (Figure 7). The problems exhibit varying levels of difficulty (Figure 8) and participants rated it as rather difficult (Figure 6, bottom-right), with an average difficulty score of 7.6 out of 10.

While we acknowledge that Bongard-RWR poses a challenge even for humans, we argue that this level of difficulty is desirable. With the rapid progress in MLLM reasoning capabilities, it is crucial to develop benchmarks that push the boundaries of current models. 

> … include standard NLP reference-based metrics ...

Thank you for this suggestion. We computed BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE_L, CIDEr,  BERTScore metrics for all tested models under Descriptive strategy. However, since these metrics primarily rely on lexical similarity, their usefulness in this setting is not obvious. For instance, the highest CIDEr score was achieved by Gemini-1.5 Pro on OpenWorld (0.13), despite underperforming (solving 32 problems in Table 1). In contrast, GPT-4 Turbo, which solved the most instances (57), had a lower CIDEr score (0.09). 
Due to space limits, we could not all results in this response. We will add and discuss them in detail the next review round.

> For the descriptive dialog strategy, …

In the Descriptive strategy, we evaluate only the final MLLM response, as depicted in Figure 2b. We will update the corresponding paragraph in Section 3.1 to make this more clear.

> What is the overlap …

We analyzed this relationship on Bongard-RWR, where we had access to instance-level human responses. Figure 8 (Appendix B) presents a heatmap with the number of human evaluators who successfully solved each problem, with red boundaries marking problems solved by at least one model. Our findings reveal notable discrepancies between human and model performance. Some problems that were relatively easy for humans (e.g. #16, #30, #47) posed significant challenges for the models. Conversely, certain problems that appeared more demanding for some human participants were successfully solved by a model (e.g., #87). This highlights certain differences in the reasoning patterns of humans and MLLMs, which we believe warrants further investigation in future works.

summary.value: The paper investigates the abstract visual reasoning capabilities of contemporary multimodal large language models (MLLMs), a problem that is aptly motivated. Firstly, the classic Bongard problems are posted to MLMMs in various forms. The machine learning models show performance that is significantly inferior to human baselines. Next, a real-world analogy, "Bongard-RWR," is designed, where experimental evaluation highlights comparable shortcomings of the MLLMs. The key result is that these models fail at Bongard problems not because of the artificial nature of the images but because of a lack of detecting and reasoning over abstract concepts altogether.

claims_and_evidence.value: The claims are appropriately supported by extensive experiments.

methods_and_evaluation_criteria.value: The possible design space of abstract visual reasoning datasets is very large. Yet, the proposed dataset is a mostly convincing construction that directly serves the dedicated purpose of assessing why MLLMs fail at Bongard-like problems. See the "Questions to Authors" below.

theoretical_claims.value: The paper does not contain mathematical theorems or proofs.

experimental_designs_or_analyses.value: The experimental design seems comprehensive. In particular, the selection of MLMMs and the different approaches to querying MLLMs are appropriate.

supplementary_material.value: The supplement consists of an extensive appendix and an online repository containing the dataset. Due to the limited time alotted to me, I only looked at them briefly and cannot suggest any improvements.

relation_to_broader_scientific_literatur.value: The relation to the wider body of work on the topic seems comprehensive.

essential_references_not_discussed.value:

Wüst, Antonia, Tim Tobiasch, Lukas Helff, Devendra S. Dhami, Constantin A. Rothkopf, Kristian Kersting (2024): *Bongard in Wonderland: Visual Puzzles that Still Make AI Go Mad?* [arXiv preprint 2410.19546v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19546).

other_strengths_and_weaknesses.value: The problem can be rather directly derived from existing work and is very significant. The overall quality and clarity are high.

Minor Comments:
- Fig. 2: The reading flow and differing visual ordering confused me.
- Fig. 4: The results are tricky to map to the experiments. For instance, it took me a bit to understand that the "Images to Sides" refers to the bottom row, not the top one.

questions_for_authors.value:
My questions center around the new dataset's solvability. The concepts in the original BPs are very clear in that there is little clutter and space for ambiguity in the clean synthetic images. However, in Bongard-RWR, the case is somewhat more ambiguous. For instance, in Fig. 1d, the triangle in the image with the candle is hard to make out as such, or in Fig. 1b, one can arguably make out more prominent lines that could count. So:

**Q1**: Did you assess to which degree humans can recognize these concepts? It appears that humans struggle significantly with the task, as indicated by the results in the last paragraph of Sec. 5. Here, humans reach 65% accuracy, whereas a random agent would already reach 30%. How do humans respond when not prompted to classify but name the rule in natural language?

summary.value: The submitted work discusses the Abstract Visual Reasoning (AVR) capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLM) with a focus on Bongard Problems (BP). To explore the gap between AVR capabilities on synthetic and real-world images, they introduce Bongard-RWR. This dataset aims to be more comparable to synthetic BPs than the state-of-the-art (Bongard-HOI and Bongard-OpenWorld) by consisting of real-world images that mirror the concepts in synthetic BPs.

claims_and_evidence.value: The paper claims to examine MLLM AVR limitations by introducing a focused real-world dataset Bongard-RWR. The intention is to facilitate direct comparisons between the synthetic and real-world domains, but, with respect to the comments below, I believe this claim is not supported sufficiently.

methods_and_evaluation_criteria.value: The presented Bongard-RWR dataset takes an interesting step in exploring the gap between reasoning on synthetic and real-world BPs. The generation of the Bongard-RWR seems plausible and justified, given the goals of the work. Nevertheless, considering the presentation in Figure 1 and the referenced github, it seems to me that the similarity between Bongard-RWR and synthetic examples could be substantially improved. For once, the real-world images do not follow the same formatting as the synthetic ones, i.e., they (i) have arbitrary aspect ratios, (ii) are not placed in the same grid, (iii) are not separated as clearly by a divider (left to right) as synthetic equivalents and (iv) do not have the same resolution. Additionally, including grayscale variants of Bongard-RWR problems in the dataset would have been appropriate to explore the gap between the synthetic and real-world problems.

theoretical_claims.value: There are no proofs or theoretical claims.

experimental_designs_or_analyses.value: The experimental design aims to show how the performance of proprietary and open MLLMs differs between synthetic BPs, state-of-the-art real-world BPs, and the proposed new dataset Bongard-RWR. The authors describe the experimental design clearly, with a granular differentiation between five modes of answer generation. With regard to the presented results, the analyses could be improved. For example, Table 1 shows the numbers of correct answers given by the MLLMs depending on dataset and answer generation strategy. However, the number of samples taken from each dataset differs (100 for prior art datasets, 60 for Bongard-RWR). This makes it less obvious to the reader to assess the relative performance difference. For example, the table shows GPT-4 Turbo is correct in 5 Bongard-HOI problems with Contrastive answer generation and in 5 Bongard-RWR problems with Descriptive answer generation. However, given the different number of overall samples, the former is correct in 5% of the cases and the latter in 0.083%. It did furthermore not become clear to me how the 100 problems of the larger datasets have been selected and why this experiment was then not repeated on different random subsets of these datasets.

supplementary_material.value: I have reviewed the appendix and the referenced Github.

relation_to_broader_scientific_literatur.value: The paper is related to prior art in two ways. First, BPs have been discussed throughout the literature as benchmark problems for visual reasoning, and this work presents an evaluation on a novel BP dataset. Second, the gap between visual reasoning capabilities on synthetic and real-world datasets is an important topic throughout the computer vision literature, including real-world variants of BPs such as the referenced Bongard-HOI and Bongard-OpenWorld datasets. In a broader context, the paper relates to the introduction of MLLMs and adds to our understanding of their visual reasoning capabilities.

other_strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
- I very much like the idea and direction this work takes, aiming to narrow down the differences between benchmarks to allow for improving our understanding of the points at which the visual reasoning capabilities of state-of-the-art models fail.
- The paper is written clearly and very easy to follow. 
- Figures 1, 2, and 3 communicate the dataset and evaluation strategies well to the reader.
- The Appendix has many interesting insights and discussions, some of which may be worth considering placing in the main paper instead to make them more visible.

Weaknesses:
- As discussed above, some easy adjustments to the dataset can further close the gap between Bongard-RWR and the synthetic dataset. Since this is the paper's primary goal, I think it is critical to address at least some of these points before publication.
- The discrepancy between the dataset sizes is a bit problematic concerning clarity. For example, while the sizes are mentioned in the caption, its not clear to the reader what the actual relative performance differences are. As a reader, with the aim of this paper in mind, I would like to be able to look at Table 1 and directly compare entries between Synthetic and RWR results.
- Similar to the point above, the discrepancies in dataset sizes may confuse the reader in Figure 4 regarding the dashed line reporting a random baseline.

summary.value:
This work evaluates vlms’ reasoning capabilities using Bongard problems. In addition to existing datasets, the authors constructed a new dataset that represents synthetic BP concepts using real-world images. Results show that some vlms can perform well if the task is simplified to binary classification, but the experiments under classical BP settings reveal vlms generally lack AVR capabilities.

## update after rebuttal
The rebuttal partly solves my concerns. I will maintain my evaluation.

claims_and_evidence.value: Most claims made are well-supported by experimental results, while it can be improved by adding more results of strong open models and using larger sample sizes.

methods_and_evaluation_criteria.value: The evaluation procedures and metrics are well designed, especially the various prompting strategies are insightful.

experimental_designs_or_analyses.value:
- It’s worth trying to feed multiple (sub-)images from group A or B all at once to vlms, which may help the models have a global understanding.
- This work uses 100 samples each from existing datasets and 60 from the constructed Bongard-RWR dataset. The sample sizes are relatively small, and thus the results may not be very stable.

supplementary_material.value: I had a quick look at most of the contents in the appendix, especially the details of the human study and the prompt formats.

relation_to_broader_scientific_literatur.value: This work can augment existing efforts to benchmark the reasoning capabilities of vlms

essential_references_not_discussed.value: This work can benefit from adding more discussion (and results) of other strong open models, including but not limited to QVQ, llama-3.2-vision, llava-onevision, etc.

other_strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
- This paper is well-written and easy to follow
- The human study is interesting, setting a valuable baseline for vlms’ reasoning capabilities evaluated by this task

other_comments_or_suggestions.value: Without comparing with the more capable open models, it’s hard to compare the difference between proprietary and open models. Some large open models can be used by api calling and should not be as expensive as proprietary models. It would be interesting to see how those strong open models perform on this task.

questions_for_authors.value: What does Bongard Problems have to offer more than existing AVR benchmarks? This is also my main concern of this paper.

summary.value:
This paper proposes a novel benchmark for multi-modal large language models based on Bongard problems.  In addition to standard Bongard problems the paper proposes "real-world" variants of such problems, where abstract images are replaced with real-world images. Furthermore, the paper proposes simpler versions of the Bongard problems where the model needs to classify correct/wrong answers instead of actually providing the answer. The paper evaluates 4 proprietary and 4 openaccess models on the proposed benchmark.

## update after rebuttal

While I am not against acceptance, I am still of the opinion that the size of the benchmark is way too small and prone to noise.

claims_and_evidence.value:
*The paper adds to the growing number of visual reasoning benchmarks on Bongard problems, e.g. "Bongard-OpenWorld: Few-Shot Reasoning for Free-form Visual Concepts in the Real World, ICLR 2024", "Bongard-HOI: Benchmarking Few-Shot Visual Reasoning for Human-Object Interactions, CVPR 2022", the novelty over these benchmarks is not clear.
* The size of the benchmark is limited, there are only 100 different problems. The small size of the benchmark would introduce noise to the results.
* The paper shows that state of the art proprietary and openaccess models do not perform well on this benchmark. Although note that these problems are inherently very challenging, with humans showing high variability in ability to solve these problems.
* The paper should include an analysis of Bongard problems that can be solved by the state of the art multi-modal LLMs. Are there any structural differences between the problems that can solved and problems that remain unsolved by all models?

methods_and_evaluation_criteria.value:
* In Figure 4, it would be interesting to include human performance, especially in the real-world image case, to quantify the difficulty level of the dataset.
* Evaluation strategy not clear: The paper should clarify the input resolution used both in case of single input images and the whole problem matrix.
* Some SOTA models are missing in the evaluation, e.g., Qwen-VL (https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-VL).

experimental_designs_or_analyses.value:
* While the paper includes extensive experiments, some SOTA models are missing in the evaluation, e.g., Qwen-VL (https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-VL).
* Due to the challenging nature of the benchmark, it would be helpful to analyze the effect of the prompt in more detail. Otherwise, the results  would conflate the effect of instruction following performance and visual reasoning performance.

supplementary_material.value: Yes, the human evaluation and dataset examples along with the code.

relation_to_broader_scientific_literatur.value: * The paper adds to the growing number of visual reasoning benchmarks on Bongard problems, e.g. "Bongard-OpenWorld: Few-Shot Reasoning for Free-form Visual Concepts in the Real World, ICLR 2024", "Bongard-HOI: Benchmarking Few-Shot Visual Reasoning for Human-Object Interactions, CVPR 2022", the novelty over these benchmarks is not clear.

essential_references_not_discussed.value: While "Winoground: Probing Vision and Language Models for Visio-Linguistic Compositionality, ICLR 2024", "Bongard-HOI: Benchmarking Few-Shot Visual Reasoning for Human-Object Interactions, CVPR 2022" are cited, the novelty over these benchmarks should be discussed in more detail.

questions_for_authors.value:
* The paper should discuss the relation to prior work on Bongard problems in more detail.
* The paper should discuss the effect of the limited size of the benchmark.
* The paper should discuss qualitative examples in the main paper, that better highlight the difficultly level of the proposed problems.

summary.value:
- The paper proposes an evaluation benchmark for assessing the visual abstraction capabilities of large multimodal models by using real-world images to mimic Bongard problems (originally formulated with synthetic images), to close the real-synth gap that can hinder evaluation. 
- The analysis uses multiple evaluation setups (e.g. where the model sees directly the Bongard image matrix and needs to output the hidden concept, or the model first captions each image independently and then provides the answer, or evaluates contrastively pairs from left-right sides etc). 
- The task is formulated either as binary classification (where the model is given a concept and needs to predict if it is correct or not), or open-ended language answer (where a majority-vote by multiple LLMs is used to score the results). 
- 4 proprietary and 4 open-sourced models are evaluated. 
- The analysis includes examples from existing Bongard sets (synthetic images, Bongard-OpenWorld, Bongard-HOI) and the newly proposed set (60 tasks created some automatically, some manually, even by photographing object configurations). 
- A human baseline is also collected for the proposed set.
- The results show that there is still a significant gap between humans and models.

## Update after rebuttal ##
I thank the authors for the detailed rebuttal.
I maintain my concerns related to the fairly low performance of the human baseline which might point to unwanted ambiguity, which, coupled with the reduced scale of the dataset, might make it hard to pinpoint causes of model failures. 
The multi-class setup is a welcome addition, to not rely exclusively on LLMs for evaluation (LLMs evolve fast, which might make it difficult to compare models over time) -- but this needs to be properly introduced and reviewed. 
I am inclined to maintain my original score.

claims_and_evidence.value:
Strengths: 
- The exercise of "translating" synthetic Bongard problems into real world images is very interesting and creative.
- The paper includes 4 proprietary and 4 open-sourced models. This is a good coverage of the model landscape.
- The different evaluation strategies (description, contrastive etc) are valuable.

Weakness:
- The first claimed contribution is confusing: “for the first time in the literature, we consider BPs in the context of MLLMs and propose…” – for analysis, the paper compiles tasks from existing benchmarks (BP-OpenWorld, BP-HOI) and adds a new set, so not sure why the proposed work is the first work to consider this set of problems.

methods_and_evaluation_criteria.value:
The authors propose binary classification and open-ended language evaluation using LLMs. 

On the binary classification task, the models are much better at recognising the negative pairings between images and concepts, than the positive ones. This could point to failure in generating realistic negative pairings. I didn’t see details on how the negative pairings were generated (but I may have missed them too, the supplementary has some 25 pages). 

For the open-language setup, I have strong concerns about using LLMs to evaluate correct answers (even by a majority voting). Given that in general LLMs struggle with nuanced descriptions of spatial relationships between objects or subtle differences, I do not consider this a robust evaluation strategy. The authors include in the appendix examples where the models and humans disagree on some answers. For the human baseline, the answers were corrected manually. Does this mean that the LLM evaluation is not robust enough? 
Wouldn’t it be possible to frame the problem as multiple-choice question answering by (manually) creating negative options that are realistic and challenging?

The human baseline is not very robust in my opinion. 30 participants were involved, mainly with academic background (Master, PhD students) – this is not representative of the human population. Even more concerning to me, even these quite highly educated participants obtained only 65% on the benchmark, with the lowest scoring about 38%. Given that these are adult individuals capable of carrying out their daily tasks puts into question the validity of the examples included in the benchmark (I myself have been confused by some examples shown in the appendix, eg 14a), and the predictive power of this benchmark (i.e. if a model performs well on this benchmark, will it perform well in real life tasks and the other way around).

In the appendix, it is mentioned that human participants were given all examples in a document and asked to submit a form? How many examples did each participant have to answer? All 60 in one session? Is there a way to check if fatigue/boredom affected their performance, e.g. if answers towards the end were more likely to be incorrect?

supplementary_material.value: I checked the supplementary material, but not the code.

questions_for_authors.value:
1. How were the negative pairings created for the binary classification setup?
2. Could the language task be formulated as multiple-choice with carefully collected realistic and challenging negative options? this would significantly reduce the ambiguity inherent in complex real world images.

title.value: Reasoning Limitations of Multimodal Large Language Models. A case study of Bongard Problems

abstract.value: Abstract visual reasoning (AVR) involves discovering shared concepts across images through analogy, akin to solving IQ test problems. Bongard Problems (BPs) remain a key challenge in AVR, requiring both visual reasoning and verbal description. We investigate whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can solve BPs by formulating a set of diverse MLLM-suited solution strategies and testing $4$ proprietary and $4$ open-access models on $3$ BP datasets featuring synthetic (classic BPs) and real-world (Bongard HOI and Bongard-OpenWorld) images. Despite some successes on real-world datasets, MLLMs struggle with synthetic BPs. To explore this gap, we introduce Bongard-RWR, a dataset representing synthetic BP concepts using real-world images. Our findings suggest that weak MLLM performance on classical BPs is not due to the domain specificity, but rather comes from their general AVR limitations. Code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/pavonism/bongard-rwr

lay_summary.value: Humans are good at recognizing abstract patterns in images, like those found in IQ tests. But can advanced AI models do the same? Our study investigates whether multimodal large language models that can process both images and text can solve Bongard Problems, a type of visual-textual reasoning challenge. We tested several advanced AI models on tasks involving synthetic and real-world images. While these models showed some success with real-world tasks, they struggled with synthetic puzzles, which are more abstract. To probe this issue, we created Bongard-RWR, a new dataset representing abstract concepts with real-world images. Our findings suggest that the AI models’ difficulties aren't just because of an unfamiliar synthetic image domain, but stem from fundamental limitations in how they understand visual concepts. This highlights the need to improve abstract reasoning capabilities of these models, a step toward more human-like reasoning.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.now())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.now().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
